newsitem.title: FRANCE: French appeals court cuts Scientology sentences.
newsitem.headline: French appeals court cuts Scientology sentences.

text.p: An appeals court on Monday spared a former leader of the Church of Scientology in Lyon, central France, from going to jail on charges of manslaughter and fraud after the suicide of a church follower.

The Lyon court gave Jean-Jacques Mazier a three-year suspended term and fined him 500,000 francs ($80,000). In October, a lower court had sentenced him to 18 months in prison, with another 18 months suspended.

The court also acquitted nine of 14 other defendants tied to the organisation who had been sentenced with Mazier on charges ranging from embezzlement to fraud. Mazier said he would make a final plea for a retrial to France's supreme court.
The five remaining defendants also received lighter sentences ranging from eight months to one year suspended with fines from 10,000 to 20,000 francs.
"This judgment implies full religious recognition of scientology in France," said Marc Bromberg, a spokesman for the church. "The Lyon appeals court has shown good sense."
At the original trial, Mazier was found guilty of manslaughter and fraud in the 1988 suicide of scientology follower Patrice Vic.
The prosecution said Mazier went to the home of Vic, a 31-year-old industrial designer, where both Mazier and Vic put pressure on Vic's wife, Nelly, to lend him money to attend a scientology course.
Unable to raise the money, Vic threw himself off his high-rise apartment block in the middle of the night.
The lawyer for Nelly Vic, who had filed charges against the Church of Scientology, also voiced satisfaction with the verdict. "Manslaughter has been acknowledged. That's the main thing," he said.

At the original trial, prosecutors portrayed the organisation as an enterprise masquerading as a religion, whose chief function was to extort cash from the gullible using abusive high-pressure techniques.
Defence lawyers argued that the church was a legitimate religion and blamed Vic's suicide on long-term depression and alcohol abuse.

The trial revolved around whether the Church of Scientology, founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard, was a sect or a religion. As a religion, it could legally ask members for funds.

The church claims more than eight million followers worldwide, including 40,000 in France. One of its teachings is that the problems of the human race are linked to disembodied souls brought to the planet millions of years ago.
Members include Hollywood film stars Tom Cruise, his Australian-born wife Nicole Kidman, John Travolta, Kirstie Alley and Lisa Marie Presley, daughter of legendary rock star Elvis.
